procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Special Judge for SPE and ACB Cases, City Civil Court, Hyderabad (trial Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 2nd August, 2022 passed by the High Court of Telangana at Hyderabad in Criminal Appeal No.1036 of 2008, dismissing the appeal of Accused Officer No.1 (AO1) and affirming the trial court's judgment dated 5th August, 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Both AO1 and AO2 filed separate appeals before the High Court of Telangana challenging the trial court's judgment. The High Court accepted the appeal of AO2 but rejected the appeal of AO1.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: AO1 (the appellant) approached the Supreme Court by filing a special leave petition challenging the High Court's judgment that dismissed his appeal and affirmed his conviction by the trial court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution was able to prove beyond all manner of doubt the fact that the appellant demanded and accepted bribe from the complainant.

facts: The appellant, a Forest Section Officer, was accused of demanding and accepting a bribe from a complainant who operated a saw-mill.
The prosecution alleged that after a fine was imposed on the saw-mill, the appellant demanded a monthly bribe.
A trap was organized by the Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP), during which the appellant was alleged to have accepted the bribe money.
The appellant's defense was that he refused the bribe and that the complainant had the opportunity to plant the tainted money in his bag, which the appellant had forgotten in a coffee shop.
law: To secure a conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, the prosecution must prove both the demand of illegal gratification and its subsequent acceptance by the accused.
This proof must be beyond all manner of doubt and can be established through either direct or circumstantial evidence.
application: The Court found that the prosecution "miserably failed" to prove the demand for the bribe with any reliable evidence. It noted that the police made no effort to record any conversations between the complainant and the appellant to verify the demand.

The evidence for the acceptance of the bribe was also found to be weak. It primarily rested on the testimony of the complainant (PW-1) and his close friend (PW-2). The Court considered PW-2 to be an "interested witness" due to his friendship with the complainant.

Crucially, the Court noted that the complainant admitted to picking up the appellant's bag, giving him a clear opportunity to "plant the tainted currency notes" inside it. There was no satisfactory evidence that the appellant had actually handled the money.

The Court heavily criticized the investigation process. The DySP registered the case and set up the trap based on the "mere ipse dixit" (unsupported assertion) of the complainant, without any preliminary verification.
Furthermore, the DySP failed to associate an independent person as a shadow witness for the trap, relying only on the complainant's friend (PW-2).

The Court also found that other evidence, such as call detail records, "completely demolish the complainant’s case" and that the manner in which another witness was involved created a "grave doubt that the entire case was orchestrated against the appellant."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution's case was full of embellishments, contradictions, and grave doubts. It held that the prosecution failed to prove the demand and acceptance of the bribe with unimpeachable evidence. Finding it unsafe to convict the appellant on such flawed evidence, the Court acquitted him of all charges and set aside the lower courts' judgments.

issue.issue_text: Whether the courts below were justified in convicting and sentencing the appellant for offence punishable u/ss.7 and 13(1)(d) r/w 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, for the demand and acceptance of illegal gratification.

facts: The appellant, a Forest Section Officer, was accused of demanding and accepting a monthly bribe of Rs. 5,000 from a saw-mill operator (the complainant).
This demand allegedly followed an incident where the appellant's squad had imposed a Rs. 50,000 fine on the saw-mill for possessing illegal teakwood.
A trap was organized by the Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) based on the complainant's allegations, leading to the appellant's arrest.
The trial court convicted the appellant, and the High Court upheld the conviction.
law: Under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, the prosecution must prove both the demand and the subsequent acceptance of the illegal gratification as a fact in issue.
Mere acceptance or receipt of money, without proof of a prior demand, is insufficient to establish the offence.
The prosecution must prove its case beyond all manner of doubt, and this can be done through either direct or circumstantial evidence.
application: The Court found the prosecution's case to be highly suspicious and full of contradictions.
It held that the prosecution "miserably failed" to prove the crucial element of demand through any reliable evidence.
The Court noted several major flaws in the prosecution's case:
- The primary witness (PW-2) to the transaction was a close friend of the complainant and therefore considered an "interested witness" rather than an independent one.
- The DySP made no effort to associate an independent person to act as a shadow witness in the trap proceedings.
- There was no satisfactory evidence to prove that the appellant had actually handled the tainted currency notes.
- The Court criticized the DySP for registering the FIR and setting up the trap based solely on the complainant's word, without any preliminary verification.
- Call detail records were found to "completely demolish" the complainant's version of events.
- The manner in which a saw-mill worker was made a panch witness raised doubts that the entire case might have been orchestrated against the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the charges of demand and acceptance of a bribe with unimpeachable evidence and beyond a reasonable doubt. Due to the numerous contradictions, embellishments, and lack of credible evidence, the Court found it unsafe to uphold the conviction. Therefore, it rejected the findings of the lower courts, acquitted the appellant, and set aside his conviction and sentence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution was able to prove beyond all manner of doubt the fact that the appellant demanded and accepted bribe from the complainant.
appellant_arguments: The allegation of acceptance of illegal gratification is surrounded by doubt.
The prosecution failed to get the hand wash of the appellant tested by the FSL, resulting in a lack of corroborative evidence that the appellant handled the tainted currency notes.
The Trap Laying Officer (TLO) was obligated to send an independent shadow witness but failed to do so.
respondent_arguments: During post-trap proceedings, the appellant admitted to receiving the money, offering a far-fetched explanation that it was a compounding fee for a non-existent case, and this admission can be used against him.
The appellant's subsequent defense that the complainant planted the money in his bag is frivolous and unacceptable.
The appellant failed to offer a plausible explanation for the tainted currency notes found in his possession and for the presence of phenolphthalein on his hand.

cases.case_name: Neeraj Dutta v. State (Government of NCT of Delhi)
cases.principle: Whether circumstantial evidence can be relied upon to prove the demand of illegal gratification and whether it is permissible to draw an inferential deduction of culpability/guilt of a public servant under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the Act based on other evidence, in the absence of direct or primary evidence from the complainant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court may raise a discretionary and rebuttable presumption of fact regarding the demand and acceptance of illegal gratification only after the foundational facts have been proven by relevant evidence. This discretionary presumption of fact is distinct from the mandatory presumption in law under Section 20 of the Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In wake of the discussion made hereinabove, we are of the view that the prosecution has failed to bring home the charges against the appellant (AO1) by leading evidence which can be termed to be of unimpeachable character. The AO1 (appellant), therefore, deserves to be acquitted of the charges.
legal_tests_applied: In order to bring home the guilt of the accused, the prosecution has to prove the demand of illegal gratification and the subsequent acceptance, by either direct or circumstantial evidence.
